summary: For ages 7–9: the ocean moves in three ways, each with its own main cause — tides (the regular, roughly twice-daily rise and fall of the whole sea, caused mainly by the Moon's gravity), waves (quick surface movement made by wind blowing across the water, where energy travels but the water mostly stays put and bobs), and currents (large, steady flows pushed by steady winds and by differences in water temperature and saltiness, which carry warmth and nutrients — and the water itself — around the globe). The central goal is matching each phenomenon to its main cause and NOT conflating them — especially the classic errors 'the wind causes the tide', 'tides and waves are the same', and 'a wave carries the water forward'. Keep the tide mechanism at the simple 'the Moon pulls the water into a bulge' level; the two-bulge model and full Sun detail come later.
misconceptions: Conflating the three — e.g. thinking tides and waves are the same thing, or that waves are caused by the Moon.
'A wave carries the water forward across the sea' — not grasping that the energy travels while the water mostly bobs in place.
'Tides are caused by wind' or 'by the Earth spinning only' — missing the Moon's gravity as the main cause.
'Currents are just where it's windy' — not seeing them as sustained global flows carrying heat and nutrients.
'The Sun has nothing to do with tides' / treating tides as irregular rather than a predictable twice-daily rhythm.

activities.title: Three dials for the sea: drive each cause, see a different effect
steps: Spin the Earth under the Moon and watch the ocean bulge stay facing the Moon while a harbour's water rises as it passes under the bulge and falls as it moves away. Real tides keep a predictable clock of about twice a day (roughly every 12½ hours); this simple one-bulge picture shows only one of those high tides.
Turn up a wind control and watch waves grow across the surface while a tethered float lifts and drops in place without travelling along with the wave.
Launch a current across a world map and watch it carry warm/cold colour and drifting nutrient particles across the globe.
After each, state the cause–effect in one sentence: Moon→tide, wind→wave, steady winds and warm/cold, salty water differences→current.
Say in your own words what travels in a wave (energy, while the water mostly stays and bobs) versus what a current carries (heat, nutrients, and even the water itself).
activities.insight: Tides, waves and currents are three different movements, each with its own main cause (the Moon for tides, wind for waves, steady winds and temperature/saltiness differences for currents); a wave moves energy while the water mostly stays in place, whereas a current actually transports water, heat and nutrients across the planet.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: three cause–effect stories
steps: Look at three panels — a Moon–Earth–water bulge, a wind-made wave, and a world current map — and tap each cause to reveal 'what makes this happen?'.
On the current map, tap warm and cold flows and name what they carry (heat and nutrients).
Match three cards: Moon→tide, wind→wave, steady winds and warm/cold, salty water differences→current, and read each back as a full sentence.
activities.insight: Each sea movement has its own clear cause, and the three can be stated as separate cause–effect stories.

activities.title: Blow across a tray of water: predict, observe, explain
steps: With a shallow tray of water, predict what will happen if you blow gently across the surface, and say why.
Blow and observe the ripples/small waves travelling across.
Explain which of the three movements you just made — a tide, a wave, or a current — and decide whether your breath could have caused a real tide.

Discuss the probes: on a still, windless day would there still be a tide? What in the sky is regular enough to set the tide timetable? If the waves are huge, does that tell you whether it's high or low tide?
activities.insight: Breath (wind) makes waves, not tides; the tide follows the Moon on a predictable timetable whether it is windy or calm (strong storms can push water a little higher or lower, but they do not make the tide), so wind strength does not tell you the tide state.

activities.title: Beach reasoning: is it the wind, the Moon, or something else?
steps: Consider: in the morning the sand is wide and dry; by teatime the sea has crept right up. A child says 'the wind blew the water up the beach.' Decide whether you agree that wind causes the tide.
Explain what actually causes the tide if the wind isn't the reason, and how a tide is different from the waves you jump in.
Answer: could a current carry a message in a bottle across a whole ocean, and how is that different from a wave?
Decide which movement the Sun's gravity also helps cause — the tides — while recognising that the Moon is the closer, dominant cause of the tides.
activities.insight: A child who assigns the tide to the Moon, waves to the wind, and currents to steady winds and temperature/saltiness differences — and can keep them distinct across new cases — has the concept; attributing the tide to wind is the gap to correct.

checkQuestion: At the beach in the morning the sand is wide and dry; by teatime the sea has crept right up and covered it. A child says 'that's because the wind blew the water up the beach'. Do you agree that the wind causes the tide — and if the wind isn't the reason, what is, and how is a tide different from the waves you jump in?
checkAnswer: The wind does NOT cause the tide. Tides — the slow, twice-a-day rise and fall of the whole sea — are caused mainly by the pull of the Moon's gravity (and a bit the Sun's) on the ocean. Waves are different: those ARE usually made by wind blowing across the water's surface, and they are quick and local. Currents are like rivers of water moving through the ocean, driven by wind at the surface and by differences in temperature and saltiness deeper down. So tide, wave and current are three different movements with three different causes.
